newsitem.title: ZAIRE: "Non-armed" opposition demands place at Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: "Non-armed" opposition demands place at Zaire talks.

text.p: Zaire's radical opposition on Thursday demanded a seat at any negotiations between President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila on ending the civil war in Zaire.
In Cape Town, the U.N.'s special envoy on Zaire said Mobutu and Kabila had agreed in principle to meet for talks.

"The outcome we have today (is) the agreement in principle by the two parties to meet at the highest level ... to discuss transitional arrangements," U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun told a news conference.

In Kinshasa, powerful opposition member of parliament Andre Boboliko told Reuters the radical opposition led by populist former prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi was entitled to join the talks because of its long campaign for democracy.
"There is an armed opposition, a non-armed opposition and those in power. Real negotiations have to include all three forces," said Boboliko, a deputy speaker of parliament.

Another senior opposition figure and member of parliament, Joseph Olenghankoy, even predicted Zaire would be ungovernable if rebels eventually wrested power and excluded the civil opposition from power.
"The rebels must understand that there is a democratic opposition which has always battled inside the country," Olenghankoy told BBC Africa Service radio.

"If one believes that a solution is Kabila-Mobutu, even if Kabila comes to take over the (capital) town after Mobutu and installs himself in power, I assure you that this country will never be governable," he added.
Kabila, whose forces hold about half Zaire, left Cape Town on Thursday after talks with South African President Nelson Mandela, whose country is mediating in the Zaire conflict.

While rebels advance on Kinshasa, Mobutu's government is facing mounting pressure from the pro-Tshisekedi opposition, which brought Kinshasa to a standstill on Monday and Tuesday with anti-Mobutu protest action.

Political analysts say Monday's stay-at-home protest and other measures planned by the opposition are intended to demonstrate to Kabila that Tshisekedi is a force to be reckoned with in future power sharing.
